format.label: A memo to a CMO
format.instruction: Write it as a short internal memo to a chief marketing officer. Plain language, no jargon they would have to look up. Around 120 words.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Memo — measuring what ads actually cause

I don't think we get placement-level truth back. The platforms have decided that's their business, not ours. So I'd stop auditing inside the black box and change what we measure.

Three moves:

1. Make testing permanent infrastructure, not a project. A standing calendar of rotating geo holdouts, roughly 10% of markets always dark somewhere, reading continuously instead of waiting weeks per answer.
2. Only ask questions at the level we can act on: how much to each platform, not which placement worked.
3. Use a model to carry test results between reads — calibrated by our experiments, never trusted alone.

Expect trouble: small channels stay unmeasurable, platforms will change behavior mid-flight, and holding spend back feels like losing money. I'd rather have wide honest ranges than precise fiction.
answers.first_move: Put a small, always-on set of markets on holdout so we start generating our own evidence instead of reading the platforms' homework.
answers.hardest_part: Small channels and short windows simply don't contain enough signal to detect the effect sizes we care about, no matter how clever the method.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
To: CMO
Subject: Measuring what ads actually caused

I would not promise a universal attribution system. The useful target is narrower: determine whether moving the next dollar is likely to create additional sales, and state the uncertainty.

Start with one large, reversible budget decision. Build an independent record of spend, platform settings, promotions, prices, inventory, and first-party sales. Run small, persistent control groups where feasible, then add planned budget changes across matched markets and time windows. Use marketing-mix models only to connect these sparse tests, never as ground truth. Require methods to predict unseen periods and recover effects from simulated and known changes; publish disagreement rather than averaging it away.

The hard limit is missing exposure data and platforms changing behavior. Some decisions will remain unknowable. In those cases, set bounds, favor reversible moves, and price better measurement into media contracts.
answers.first_move: Choose one large, reversible budget decision and define what evidence would change it.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is separating real advertising impact from platform behavior when the platforms control both delivery and the evidence.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: Memo to CMO: We cannot measure what black-box ad platforms cause on a daily basis, and anyone selling a unified attribution model is guessing. The platforms deliberately hide granular data and change their internal algorithms without telling us, breaking standard statistical models. Instead of chasing impossible precision, we should treat spend like an uncertain financial portfolio. I would stop trying to micro-steer automated campaigns and focus on measuring gross business impact through occasional, aggressive budget cutbacks in selected regional pockets. We then compare those dips against our baseline organic sales. This will give us fewer readings and less false precision, but the signals we get will reflect reality rather than modeled platform assumptions.
answers.first_move: Turn off ad spend completely in three mid-sized sales regions for two weeks to measure our true baseline demand without paid media.
answers.hardest_part: Ad platforms constantly shift their optimization algorithms mid-flight, quietly destroying the historical stability that statistical measurement requires.

format.label: Three moves
format.instruction: Give exactly three moves, in order. One sentence each, then one sentence on what makes that move hard. Nothing else.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Move 1 — Build a trustworthy dependent variable before any model: one deduped first-party outcome series at the finest geo-by-day grain you can defend, with lag curves estimated and offline/CRM conversions stitched in, and stop treating platform-reported conversions as anything other than a bidding telemetry feed. What makes it hard: your own measurement degrades non-randomly across exactly the channels you're comparing, so the errors correlate with the treatment and quietly bias every causal read downstream.

Move 2 — Stop trying to audit the black box and instead permanently tax the media plan (roughly 5–10%) for always-on budget perturbation — staggered geo rotations, switchbacks, and small randomized spend steps running continuously — so you are estimating the local slope of response to the next dollar rather than trying to recover placement- or query-level truth that no longer exists. What makes it hard: it requires the organization to accept deliberate, permanent, visible suboptimality, and the reads are contaminated by learning-phase resets, cross-geo spillover, and the platform reallocating around your perturbation in ways that mimic the effect you are measuring.

Move 3 — Replace the single MMM answer with an arbitration rule: run MMM, geo-lift, and perturbation slopes in parallel, act only where two of three agree on sign and rough magnitude, cap each reallocation to the size the evidence can actually support, and make the benchmark prospective — does the model predict the outcome of next quarter's perturbations, not does it fit history. What makes it hard: the honest output is often "we can't tell," which is organizationally unacceptable, and non-stationarity means a model can fail validation for reasons that have nothing to do with the model being wrong when it was built.
answers.first_move: Fix and consolidate the conversion data we actually own, before touching any model.
answers.hardest_part: The system you are measuring changes its own behavior while you measure it, so no estimate stays true long enough to be validated by the standards we'd normally demand.

What makes this hard is that consequential optimization changes remain latent, so some treatment versions will be unknowable rather than merely noisy. Move 2: Run continuous randomized budget or eligibility perturbations across many small geo, time, product, or audience cells, then estimate dynamic effects with partial pooling instead of waiting for occasional campaign-scale holdouts. What makes this hard is that interference, carryover, low power, and optimizer adaptation can turn each perturbation into a changing policy treatment rather than a clean channel test. Move 3: Create a validation regime that preregisters predictions from competing causal models and scores their interval coverage against the rarer, larger holdouts, retaining only methods that remain calibrated across platform regime changes. What makes this hard is that experiments are the only credible ground truth yet are scarce, imperfect, and often not transportable to the next optimization regime.
answers.first_move: Define exactly which buying-policy effect the system is supposed to estimate.
answers.hardest_part: The treatment itself changes as platform optimizers react, while the data needed to observe that change is withheld.

What makes this hard is that automated bidding algorithms penalize budget volatility by constantly resetting learning states, which degrades live delivery efficiency during the test. 2. Build an independent baseline forecast of organic customer conversion velocity and repeat purchases using only first-party transaction timing, completely ignoring ad telemetry. What makes this hard is that automated platforms actively target users with the highest baseline intent to convert, making organic demand mathematically non-identifiable from algorithmic demand capture without true counterfactual data. 3. Calibrate macro media mix models exclusively against coarse, high-magnitude portfolio spend pauses while treating remaining platform-specific attribution as directional noise. What makes this hard is that commercial stakeholders routinely reject wide credible intervals and deliberate revenue loss from spend pauses in favor of the comforting illusion of precise platform attribution.
answers.first_move: Run synchronized, high-magnitude budget pulses across all automated channels at once to measure total portfolio elasticity instead of channel attribution.
answers.hardest_part: Ad platform algorithms actively target people who are already about to buy, making causal incrementality mathematically impossible to isolate from baseline intent without continuous, revenue-damaging holdouts.

format.label: Pseudocode
format.instruction: Express the approach as short annotated pseudocode. The comments should carry the reasoning; the code should carry the structure. Around 15 lines.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
```
# 0. Give up the audit. Placement/query diagnostics are gone for good; chasing them is sunk cost.
#    Treat each buying surface as ONE actuator with ONE dial. Measurement granularity should equal
#    steering granularity -- anything finer is a number you cannot act on anyway.
ACTUATORS = [pmax_us, adv_plus_prospect, tiktok_smart, ...]   # not "channels", not placements

# 1. Target the derivative, not the level. "What did Meta contribute?" is unidentifiable at most budgets;
#    "what does the next $10k on this actuator do" is both cheaper to identify and the only decision you have.
while always_on:                                  # episodic holdouts are dead on arrival: weeks per read,
    for a in ACTUATORS:                           # and the platform has changed by the time you read it
        perturb(a, design=switchback(geo_clusters, period=5d, amplitude=+/-20%, randomize_order))
        # expect: reflexivity. Your perturbation triggers re-learning, so you measure a system you disturbed.
        # Mitigate with amplitude caps + burn-in windows, never fully solve. Report it as bias, not noise.

# 2. Power: one advertiser cannot power one channel read. Stop pretending. Pool instead.
priors = hierarchical_fit(every_experiment_ever_run, levels=[vertical, actuator, spend_decile, season])
# expect: over half of actuator-weeks never individually identify. Shrink hard toward pooled prior and
# publish the shrinkage. A wide honest interval beats a narrow self-attributed one.

# 3. Demote MMM to an interpolator between experiments. It is bookkeeping, not causal inference.
mmm = fit(sales ~ spend, priors=priors, regimes=platform_change_log)   # log every product/policy change
# expect: stationarity still breaks. Prefer explicit change-points over longer lookbacks; refit weekly.

# 4. The actual missing artifact is a benchmark, not a better model. Build one in-house.
held_out = reserve(experiments, 20%, never_seen_by_model)
score = oos_error(mmm.predict_lift(held_out.design), held_out.observed_lift)
assert_no_number_ships_without(score)   # makes vendor disagreement testable instead of rhetorical

# 5. Never calibrate to platform-reported conversions. Use them only as a covariate whose bias you estimate.
```
answers.first_move: Write down every dial you can actually turn on each platform, and throw out any measurement ambition finer than that list.
answers.hardest_part: The act of experimenting changes the algorithm you are trying to measure, so the estimate and the system drift together and there is no clean counterfactual to converge on.

format.label: A checklist
format.instruction: Give a checklist someone could actually run next quarter. Each item concrete enough to be marked done or not done. Six items at most.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
1. **Decision inventory + power audit (weeks 1–3).** List every budget or bid decision you would actually change in the next two quarters, with the dollar size of each. For each, compute the MDE a geo or switchback design could detect given your conversion volume and geo variance. Output a signed two-column doc: *measurable* vs. *declared unmeasurable*. I disagree with the reflex to chase channel-level incrementality for everything — anything under roughly 10–15% of spend will not produce a read, and pretending otherwise is where these programs die. Put those lines on a portfolio heuristic and stop paying for measurement on them. Done = doc exists, each line has an MDE and a named decision owner.

2. **One always-on rotation on your biggest black box (live by week 6, first read by week 10).** Not an on/off holdout — a staggered geo rotation testing *spend levels* (e.g. −40% cells), rotating cells every 3–4 weeks so reads accumulate rather than arriving once. Test at the platform-total level, not per-campaign: PMax/Advantage+ cannibalize branded search and retargeting, so anything narrower is confounded by design. Done = rotation running, pre-registered analysis plan committed before unblinding, first read delivered and second rotation started.

3. **Platform regime telemetry (weeks 2–6).** Daily capture of every delivery field still exposed (CPM, impression share, geo/device mix, asset-group spend split, whatever the API still returns), plus a manual log of platform announcements and your own account changes. Run simple changepoint detection on the series. Every measurement read you publish carries a validity window and a note on whether a break occurred inside it. This is the cheapest item here and the most neglected — it's what stops you from re-litigating a model that was fine until the platform changed under it. Done = dashboard live, at least one break detected and written up.

4. **Change what the box maximizes instead of auditing it (weeks 4–10).** You cannot see placements; you can change the objective. Ship server-side conversion imports carrying your own values — margin, new-vs-existing, experiment-adjusted incremental value — replacing platform-default conversion values in one platform. Then test the swap itself with a geo rotation, because it is a real intervention with a real lift number. This is the highest-leverage steering lever left and it doesn't depend on winning any argument about attribution.

5. **Score models, don't compare them (weeks 8–12).** Hold back at least two completed experiment reads. Require every candidate — Meridian, Robyn, each vendor, in-house — to predict those lifts out-of-sample before seeing them, same data, same window. Publish the errors. Expect wide intervals and at least one vendor to decline; both are informative. Done = a scorecard with numbers per candidate and a written rule for which model informs which decision, at what weight.

6. **Pre-commit the reallocation policy (week 12).** Budget moves are bounded by evidence tier: experiment-backed lines can move freely, model-backed lines within ±15%, platform-reported-only lines within ±5% and only with a scheduled re-test. Attach a standing cadence so the rotation from item 2 never goes dark. This is the part teams skip, and it's why good reads change nothing. Done = policy signed by whoever owns the budget, and one reallocation executed under it.

What I expect to break: geo granularity will be unusable on at least one major platform; spillover between adjacent DMAs will eat some of your power; and the value-signal swap in item 4 will look like a performance drop for 2–3 weeks while the algorithm re-learns, which will create pressure to abort before the read. Decide in advance who has authority to hold the line.
answers.first_move: Write down the specific budget decisions you would actually change next quarter, and check whether you have enough conversions to detect a difference on each one.
answers.hardest_part: The measurement target is a moving, self-interested system — the platform changes its own behavior mid-flight and controls what you're allowed to see, so there is no stable thing to estimate and no ground truth to validate against except experiments you mostly can't afford to power.

answers.approach:
- [ ] **Write a measurement contract for each decision.** Name the intervention, counterfactual, business outcome, time horizon, and minimum detectable lift—for example, “incremental 28-day gross profit from allowing PMax to spend the next $250k.” Reject platform-attributed conversions as the outcome source.
- [ ] **Create a dated intervention and change-point ledger.** Log budgets, eligibility, audiences, objectives, conversion definitions, consent changes, promotions, and every observable platform-model change. Add automated alerts for discontinuities in spend, reach, CPM, conversion rate, and channel overlap.
- [ ] **Complete a power and interference audit before testing.** Evaluate geo tests, audience holdouts, switchbacks, budget pulses, matched-market tests, and platform conversion-lift studies. Document which are identifiable, which risk cross-cell contamination, and which cannot detect the minimum useful effect. Do not run an underpowered geo test merely to claim experimentation.
- [ ] **Run two or three deliberately different interventions.** Prefer randomized channel eligibility or suppression where available; otherwise use precommitted budget or time-based perturbations with guardrails. Measure total business outcomes and the optimizer’s adaptation path, not placement-level effects the platform no longer exposes.
- [ ] **Hold out at least one experiment from model fitting.** Fit multiple MMM or causal time-series specifications using identical data and declared priors, calibrate only on the remaining tests, then score predictions against the held-out intervention. Publish sign accuracy, interval coverage, effect error, and sensitivity to change-point assumptions. I disagree with treating experiments only as calibration inputs—they are more valuable as scarce out-of-sample validation.
- [ ] **Adopt only decision rules that survive triangulation.** Permit budget changes only when experimental evidence, model direction, and business-outcome trends agree within predefined tolerances; otherwise label the result unresolved and preserve exploration spend. End the quarter with a reproducible evidence table, not a single “true” cross-channel attribution number.

format.label: A lullaby
format.instruction: Write it as a short lullaby: three or four gentle rhyming couplets someone could actually sing. Soft on the surface, honest underneath. The problem is still unsolved when the song ends, and the song should know it.

answers.label: Claude

Hush now, the dashboard is glowing so green, / but green is a guess at a thing never seen. / So hold back a few little cities tonight, / and never un-hold them — that's how we find light. // Don't ask the big model to tell you what's true; / it only compresses the small tests you do. / Sleep, love; it re-learns itself while you dream, / so nothing stays measured as long as it seems.

(Sung plainly: a permanent, always-on geo holdout — a standing measurement tax of five or ten percent, budgeted like rent, not run like a project — is the only unbiased signal you own. I'd disagree with the obvious move, which is to make MMM the arbiter: MMM is a compression layer over experiments, not a replacement for them, and an uncalibrated MMM is a vendor's prior wearing your data as a costume. Ladder it: cheap, frequent, low-power reads that you never stop, pooled over time into a prior rather than read one at a time; treat the platform itself as the unit of analysis, not the channel; and re-run the standing test after every optimization change, because the thing you measured last quarter no longer exists. Expect: underpowered reads for most line items, ugly fights about opportunity cost of the holdout, and an honest ceiling of decision-grade, not truth-grade. It stays unsolved. You just get to be wrong more slowly.)
